1.pericope_label: Say ye unto your brethren, Ammi; and to your sisters, Ru–hamah. Plead with your mother, plead: for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband: let her therefore put away her whoredoms out of her sight, and her adulteries from between her breasts; Lest I strip her naked, and set her as in the day that she was born, and make her as a wilderness, and set her like a dry land, and slay her with thirst.

schools.summary: Take the mother for the nation as a collective abstract, deny that the restoration means a return of the ten tribes, and read the stripping against the exposure of a newborn.
Insist the mutual exhortation follows a divine proclamation, since men cannot make themselves God's children, and read the plea christologically.
Give the historical occasion, name the mother as a city, and press the covenant condition of walking with God.
Reads the names of mercy as restored to a spiritual Israel of Jews and Gentiles who stir one another up to walk worthy of a common salvation.

debates.question: Who is the mother that is to be pleaded with?

positions.position: The nation Israel viewed as a collective abstract, the children being the individual inhabitants.
The body of the nation, the plea being to lay before her the sin of rejecting the Messiah as the apostles did.
A city, named as Samaria in the chapter argument and as Jerusalem at the second verse.

debates.question: What does the day of her birth refer to?

positions.position: The nativity of the people in Egypt, when they had no wealth, possessions or country.
The same, with the added possibility of an allusion to female infanticide, the child abandoned to death on the day she was born.
The penalty of adultery among the ancient Germans, who stripped the offender before her relatives and drove her from the house.

outliers.claim: Argues that since the patriarchal promise of innumerable multiplication is realized through pardon and restoration, the fulfilment is not to be looked for in a return of the ten tribes, the historical books mentioning only a portion of two.
Judges that however reproachful such punishments were to the delinquent, they had no tendency to promote her moral reformation.

themes: Say ye unto your brethren, Ammi; and to your sisters, Ru–hamah.
Plead with your mother, plead: for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband: let her therefore put away her whoredoms out of her sight, and her adulteries from between her breasts;
Lest I strip her naked, and set her as in the day that she was born, and make her as a wilderness, and set her like a dry land, and slay her with thirst.

4.pericope_label: And I will not have mercy upon her children; for they be the children of whoredoms. For their mother hath played the harlot: she that conceived them hath done shamefully: for she said, I will go after my lovers, that give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, mine oil and my drink.

schools.summary: Presses the family likeness of the children to the mother into a charge against a people who love to have idolatry so, and notes the shift of person in the address.
Denies that the repentant are being told to condemn their own mother, taking the passage instead as a check on a people who contend with God as too severe.
Takes the children as consecrated to idols whose marks they bear, and refers the reader elsewhere for the inventory the mother claims.

debates.question: What makes them children of whoredoms?

positions.position: Consecration: they are idolaters dedicated to idols, whose marks they bear.
Likeness: born of doubtful parentage and personally defiled, endorsing their mother's degradation.
Succession: the posterity of the Jews in later ages, persisting in their forefathers' sins and in the rejection of the Messiah.

outliers.claim: Denies that the prophet teaches the faithful who had already repented to condemn their own mother, holding that the passage checks the waywardness of a people who never ceased contending with God as though he were more severe than just.

Locates the aggravation of the shame in the direction of the pursuit, that she seeks her lovers rather than being sought, and ascribes to them the very benefits the covenant history assigns to another hand.

themes: And I will not have mercy upon her children; for they be the children of whoredoms.

For their mother hath played the harlot: she that conceived them hath done shamefully: for she said, I will go after my lovers, that give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, mine oil and my drink.

6.pericope_label: Therefore, behold, I will hedge up thy way with thorns, and make a wall, that she shall not find her paths. And she shall follow after her lovers, but she shall not overtake them; and she shall seek them, but shall not find them: then shall she say, I will go and return to my first husband; for then was it better with me than now.

schools.summary: Makes the hedge and the wall together denote transportation into a situation where the adultery with idols could not be continued at all.
Explain the necessity of chastisement when men congratulate themselves in their vices, and infer that the following after lovers must be of the affections only.
Extends the hedge to a captivity so deep that the road home is never found.
Frames the threat by its purpose, that God warns in order not to wound and threatens in order not to strike, and notes that a promise is annexed to the threatening.

debates.question: How far does the hedge of thorns reach?

positions.position: To afflictions and wars that stop them stirring abroad, and specifically from going to the shrines of the calves or down to Egypt.
To a situation in which the adultery with the idols cannot be continued at all.
To a captivity so deep that she never finds the road back to her own land.

outliers.claim: Observes that a promise is annexed to the threatening, so that it is hard to say whether the prediction or the distress itself should be called a threatening or a promise.
Infers that since she has been hedged in and walled up she cannot go after her lovers in any proper sense, so the following after them must be understood of her affections and desires.

themes: Therefore, behold, I will hedge up thy way with thorns, and make a wall, that she shall not find her paths.

And she shall follow after her lovers, but she shall not overtake them; and she shall seek them, but shall not find them: then shall she say, I will go and return to my first husband; for then was it better with me than now.

8.pericope_label: For she did not know that I gave her corn, and wine, and oil, and multiplied her silver and gold, which they prepared for Baal. Therefore will I return, and take away my corn in the time thereof, and my wine in the season thereof, and will recover my wool and my flax given to cover her nakedness. And now will I discover her lewdness in the sight of her lovers, and none shall deliver her out of mine hand. I will also cause all her mirth to cease, her feast days, her new moons, and her sabbaths, and all her solemn feasts.

schools.summary: Corrects the tense to a present, hears in the clause a yearning that anticipates the parable of the prodigal, and defends the festal mirth as no bad sign in itself.
Finds two sins in the ignorance, the ascribing to idols and the robbing of God, and calls the whole an inexcusable stupidity in a people so taught.
Turns the ignorance into two general observations about attributing God's gifts to chance and perverting them to dishonour him.

debates.question: Who are the lovers before whom she is exposed?

positions.position: Her idols together with her allies, faithful or faithless.
Identified by the historical agency of the Assyrian king who took the goods back.
Reported as the Egyptians and Assyrians, inclined toward the Romans, and finally taken more generally of the folly of rejecting the Messiah.

outliers.claim: Derives the word for what is uncovered, occurring nowhere else, from a root meaning to be withered or faded, and takes it for a body that has suffered much defilement.

Defends the mirth as not in itself a bad sign, since David danced before the Lord and none was to appear before God with a sad countenance, and distinguishes the feast days from the more generic solemn feasts.

themes: For she did not know that I gave her corn, and wine, and oil, and multiplied her silver and gold, which they prepared for Baal.
Therefore will I return, and take away my corn in the time thereof, and my wine in the season thereof, and will recover my wool and my flax given to cover her nakedness.
And now will I discover her lewdness in the sight of her lovers, and none shall deliver her out of mine hand.
I will also cause all her mirth to cease, her feast days, her new moons, and her sabbaths, and all her solemn feasts.

12.pericope_label: And I will destroy her vines and her fig trees, whereof she hath said, These are my rewards that my lovers have given me: and I will make them a forest, and the beasts of the field shall eat them. And I will visit upon her the days of Baalim, wherein she burned incense to them, and she decked herself with her earrings and her jewels, and she went after her lovers, and forgat me, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Prefers make desolate to destroy, notes the Greek version's different reading of the following clause, and takes the plural Baalim for one deity worshipped in many places.
Supply the fulfilment from the historian and press that the visitation is a just punishment for a religion corrupted.
Take the plural for a multitude of distinct idols and read the rewards as praise given to them for all abundance.

debates.question: What does the plural Baalim denote?

positions.position: A multitude of distinct male idols, the species marked by an adjunct, as the corresponding plural covers the female ones.
One deity worshipped in different places with distinguishing local characteristics, so the compound names are local forms of one god.
The idolatries of the forefathers, for which a later generation is punished though it set up other idols of its own.

outliers.claim: Supplies the fulfilment from the historian, that trees were cut down to build forts and cast up mounts against the city, so that ground once adorned with gardens was left miserable to look at.

Repeats that when God deals severely he is visiting sins and inflicting just punishment, and observes that the prophet points as with a finger at what chiefly displeased God, that religion itself had been corrupted.

themes: And I will destroy her vines and her fig trees, whereof she hath said, These are my rewards that my lovers have given me: and I will make them a forest, and the beasts of the field shall eat them.

And I will visit upon her the days of Baalim, wherein she burned incense to them, and she decked herself with her earrings and her jewels, and she went after her lovers, and forgat me, saith the Lord.

14.pericope_label: Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably unto her.

schools.summary: Deny that the connective draws an inference from the sin, and make the exile a repetition of the wilderness in which Israel was first espoused.
Read the change of method from rough ways to gentle, and note an inversion in the clauses and the kindly sense of a verb that often means to wheedle.
Draws the whole out as an affectionate husband dealing privately with an unfaithful wife, and calls that the simple meaning of the metaphors.
Keeps the causal force of the connective and treats the result as a wonder, since after she forgot me one would expect therefore I will abandon her.

debates.question: What force has the connective that introduces the promise?

positions.position: Full causal force, and the wonder is that mercy rather than abandonment follows from the sin.
Not an inference at all: a particle used to make a strong transition, linked with what precedes without concluding from it.
Nevertheless or notwithstanding, against the assuredly of some versions.

outliers.claim: Notes an inversion in the clauses, so that God persuades her after drawing her into the desert, and observes that the verb often means to deceive or wheedle but here means to speak kindly to a rebellious people.
Carries the promise past the exile to the call of a spiritual Israel in the first times of the gospel and to the withdrawal of believing Jews to Pella before the city fell.

themes: Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably unto her.

15.pericope_label: And I will give her her vineyards from thence, and the valley of Achor for a door of hope: and she shall sing there, as in the days of her youth, and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt. And it shall be at that day, saith the Lord, that thou shalt call me Ishi; and shalt call me no more Baali.

schools.summary: Renders the phrase away from thence and sets the valley's old associations of disgrace against its new character as the threshold of a blessed life.
Take the vineyards as emblems of spiritual supply and make the change of names the first visible fruit of repentance.
Read the giving from the time of repentance, describe the valley's fruitfulness, and take the naming as a whole disposition of obedience.

positions.position: Either from the wilderness itself or from the time of her being brought there.
Away from thence: as soon as she has left the wilderness of exile and discipline.
From the time of their repentance.

outliers.claim: Takes the singing for the responsive song used at high festivals and at marriages, and notes that the Song of Solomon is a composition of that kind.
Identifies the fruit of repentance as a pure worship with all superstitions abolished, and takes the word husband as chosen to remind a corrected people of the covenant made with them.

themes: And I will give her her vineyards from thence, and the valley of Achor for a door of hope: and she shall sing there, as in the days of her youth, and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt.
And it shall be at that day, saith the Lord, that thou shalt call me Ishi; and shalt call me no more Baali.

17.pericope_label: For I will take away the names of Baalim out of her mouth, and they shall no more be remembered by their name. And in that day will I make a covenant for them with the beasts of the field, and with the fowls of heaven, and with the creeping things of the ground: and I will break the bow and the sword and the battle out of the earth, and will make them to lie down safely.

schools.summary: Make the disuse of the idols' names follow of itself once the nation stops calling God by the shared title, and set outward harmony as the counterpart of inward.
Turn the promise into a doctrine of providence, that God can arm all creatures against us or make them conducive to our safety, and guard the word covenant as a pledge of certainty.
Itemise what the covenant secures against beasts, war and robbers, and divide the fulfilment between the return from captivity and the church.

debates.question: When is the promised peace fulfilled?

positions.position: As the state the church attains once idolatry and false religion are wholly abolished.
In some measure at the return from captivity, but fully only in the church of Christ.
Wholly in the latter day, as the outward counterpart of an inward change not yet made.

outliers.claim: Reminds that the cause of all evils is that men provoke God's wrath, since he has all creatures in his hand and can arm them in vengeance or make everything in heaven and earth conducive to our safety.
Qualifies the removal of the names, holding that they would not vanish from speech but be spoken only with detestation, and extends the removal to the mouths of Gentiles as well as converted Jews.

themes: For I will take away the names of Baalim out of her mouth, and they shall no more be remembered by their name.

And in that day will I make a covenant for them with the beasts of the field, and with the fowls of heaven, and with the creeping things of the ground: and I will break the bow and the sword and the battle out of the earth, and will make them to lie down safely.

19.pericope_label: And I will betroth thee unto me for ever; yea, I will betroth thee unto me in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies. I will even betroth thee unto me in faithfulness: and thou shalt know the Lord.

schools.summary: Renders the repeated verb strictly as betrothing to oneself and lets the promise run straight on into the knowledge that follows from it.
Deny that the eternal covenant is meant, refer the betrothal to a conversion still future, and decline a refined reading of righteousness and judgment.
Reads the four terms as measures of the transaction, suggests an allusion to the betrothal dowry, and makes the knowing the guarantee against further idolatry.

debates.question: What do righteousness and judgment mean here?

positions.position: Measures of the transaction: according to law, reason and equity, and according to what is fit and becoming.
Not the refined sense of gratuitous imputation and defence against enemies, but generally that the covenant stands firm because there is truth and rectitude on both sides.
Read through the faithfulness of the following verse, which is first Christ's and only derivatively the church's.

outliers.claim: Makes the knowing the guarantee of everything else, since when the conviction that God is the sole and eternal good of the spirit is fully rooted there can be no more idolatry.
Denies that the whole body of the elect is meant, since those were betrothed in the everlasting covenant from eternity while this verse looks forward to a conversion still to come.

themes: And I will betroth thee unto me for ever; yea, I will betroth thee unto me in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies.
I will even betroth thee unto me in faithfulness: and thou shalt know the Lord.

21.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass in that day, I will hear, saith the Lord, I will hear the heavens, and they shall hear the earth; And the earth shall hear the corn, and the wine, and the oil; and they shall hear Jezreel. And I will sow her unto me in the earth; and I will have mercy upon her that had not obtained mercy; and I will say to them which were not my people, Thou art my people; and they shall say, Thou art my God.

schools.summary: Keeps the chain of hearing bare from God to heaven to earth to the produce, and points to the apostolic use of the closing promise.
Explain why the increase of people had to be added to the increase of produce, and take the sowing for a multiplication of spiritual offspring.
Trace the hearing through clouds and dry ground as supplication answered, and divide the increase between the return from captivity and the gospel.

debates.question: Has the closing promise been fulfilled?

positions.position: Yes, in the apostolic sense, when by the acceptance of Israel's hope both Jews and Gentiles are called children of the living God.
In part at the return from captivity, and much more since the preaching of the gospel.
Not yet: it does not appear that these promises have had their accomplishment.
In the latter day, at a conversion of Jews and Gentiles still to come.

outliers.claim: Explains why the increase of the people had to be promised alongside the increase of corn and wine and oil, since abundance would serve no end unless the land had numerous inhabitants, and sets this new favour against the earlier threat that only a remnant should be preserved.
Makes the name that means the seed of God the pivot of the promise, so that in the sowing it appears that mercy has been shown to those who had not obtained mercy.

themes: And it shall come to pass in that day, I will hear, saith the Lord, I will hear the heavens, and they shall hear the earth;
And the earth shall hear the corn, and the wine, and the oil; and they shall hear Jezreel.

And I will sow her unto me in the earth; and I will have mercy upon her that had not obtained mercy; and I will say to them which were not my people, Thou art my people; and they shall say, Thou art my God.
